narrative:
The model estimated a 73.2% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a high-risk prediction, not a certainty, but it was the basis for denying your law school application.

The strongest factor was your third-year academic standing: your third-year decile was 1.00, while accepted students averaged about 5.79. This pushed the prediction most strongly toward bar-exam failure. Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor and, in your case, actually worked in your favor, lowering the estimated failure risk, even though your score of 36 is slightly below the accepted-student average of about 37.18. The third most influential factor was your first-year academic standing: a decile of 3.00 versus an accepted-student average of about 6.00, which also pushed toward failure. Together, these signals led to the high predicted failure risk and the rejection.

As next steps, ask admissions whether you can discuss the decision and what evidence would strengthen a future application. Focus on improving your academic record, especially your upper-year performance, and seek structured bar-exam readiness support. Consider retaking the LSAT if you can meaningfully raise your score, and think about delaying reapplication until you can show stronger academic preparation and a clearer plan for bar success.
